38593928.finding: In five studies of donor-tissue grafts, 95.3% of patients returned to play and no graft ruptures were reported. The authors noted a lack of high-quality evidence comparing donor grafts with a patient's own tissue in elite throwers.
38593928.headline: Donor grafts for UCL reconstruction: outcomes review

38599535.finding: Across 21 studies, return-to-play rates after UCL reconstruction ranged from 62.5% to 100%, with returns at 9.5 to 18.5 months. Outcome and satisfaction scores were favorable; complication rates varied widely, from 0% to 31.8%.
38599535.headline: Tommy John surgery outcomes: what 21 studies and 2,452 patients show

38702939.finding: Across 105 articles, rehab protocols varied widely. After reconstruction, patients who reached the early milestones sooner — motion, strengthening, throwing — returned to play earlier, with no negative effect on outcome scores.
38702939.headline: Rehab timing after UCL injury: earlier milestones, earlier return

40029165.finding: Measured in a way that isolates soft tissue, the throwing shoulder's limits showed up in outward rotation rather than inward. The authors concluded that reported inward-rotation losses are not as common as once thought.
40029165.headline: How a pitcher's throwing shoulder changes over time

40744844.finding: Across 18 randomized trials (1,082 patients), platelet-rich plasma improved measured knee stability but did not significantly improve pain or function scores. The authors called for more high-quality trials.
40744844.headline: Platelet-rich plasma in ACL reconstruction: a small stability gain, mixed results

41313368.finding: Pooling 14 randomized trials (869 patients), the authors found platelet concentrates did not improve patient-reported outcomes or revision rates after ACL reconstruction. They concluded the current level I evidence does not support the add-on.
41313368.headline: Platelet concentrates in ACL reconstruction: the level I evidence check

42335646.finding: The authors described exercise as a controlled stress that shifts immune cells toward repair mode. That shift creates the conditions that switch on satellite cells, the stem cells that rebuild muscle.
42335646.headline: How exercise retrains the immune system to help muscle regrow

42463241.finding: The review found that satellite cells — the muscle's resident stem cells — decline in number and repair power with age, which diminished the muscle's ability to recover from injury. The authors noted the causes in humans are not yet fully understood.
42463241.headline: Muscle stem cells weaken with age

42515772.finding: Across aging and several chronic diseases, the review found the same barriers to muscle repair: long-running inflammation, metabolic problems, and scar-like tissue buildup. The authors noted that treatments aimed at several barriers at once looked promising in early studies, but clinical evidence is still limited.
42515772.headline: Why muscle repair slows in aging and chronic disease

42564996.finding: Healthy youth and high school players had slightly more hip rotation than injured players. The authors concluded the differences were small and the studies mixed, so no strong recommendation can be made yet.
42564996.headline: Hip motion and injury risk in baseball players

42925023.finding: In 187 collegiate pitchers followed for one summer, arm injury risk rose when a pitcher's pitch counts climbed above his own usual workload. Injuries were also linked to drops in fastball velocity.
42925023.headline: Pitch-count jumps and velocity drops linked to arm injuries in college pitchers

42963566.finding: Reviewing 419 studies, the authors found the strongest support for human donor grafts and a patient's own tissue in high-risk rotator cuff repairs. Evidence for platelet-rich plasma and stem cells was inconsistent, and no single approach was best for every repair.
42963566.headline: Added tissue and biologics for rotator cuff repair: what the evidence supports
